publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: method
span.quote: The main conceptual contribution of this paper is a framework for fair classification comprising (1) a (hypothetical) task-specific metric for determining the degree to which individuals are similar with respect to the classification task at hand; (2) an algorithm for maximizing utility subject to the fairness constraint, that similar individuals are treated similarly.

span.label: fairness in classification
span.quote: In this work, we study fairness in classification.

span.label: formal-framework
span.quote: Our framework permits us to formulate the question as an optimization problem that can be solved by a linear program.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: fairness as treat similar individuals similarly, formalized as a Lipschitz condition on the classifier w.r.t. a task-specific similarity metric, maximizing utility subject to that constraint
span.quote: We formalize this guiding principle as a Lipschitz condition on the classifier

span.label: the approach assumes a task-specific similarity metric, which is hard to define
span.quote: a task-specific similarity metric describing the extent to which pairs of individuals should be regarded as similar

span.label: Obtaining or justifying the task-specific similarity metric the framework depends on is the hardest part, and any real metric will be an approximation.
span.quote: Justifying the availability of or access to the distance metric in various settings is one of the most challenging aspects of our framework, and in reality the metric used will most likely only be society’s current best approximation to the truth.

span.label: The general fairness LP gives no quantitative bound on the loss it incurs.
span.quote: The result however does not give a concrete quantitative bound on the resulting loss.

span.label: When the protected set is far from the rest of the population under the metric, satisfying the Lipschitz condition can still leave unfair practices unchecked.
span.quote: Thus, if members of S are relatively far from the members of T according to the distance metric, then satisfying the Lipschitz condition may fail to prevent some of the unfair practices.

span.label: No tight Earthmover characterisation is obtained for the relative-infinity distance version of the bias.
span.quote: The situation for biasD∞, d is somewhat more complicated and we do not get a tight characterization in terms of an Earthmover distance.

span.label: The whole treatment assumes one metric applied uniformly to everyone; per-user or plural metrics are untested.
span.quote: Further research into the feasibility of this approach is needed, in particular, our discussion throughout this paper has assumed that a single metric is used across the board.

span.label: The nearest existing similarity system the authors point to (AALIM, health care) does not supply the kind of distance metric the framework needs.
span.quote: This work could serve as a starting point in the fairness setting, although it does not (yet?) provide the distance metric that our approach requires.

span.label: A widely used fairness criterion can hold while the outcome is, in the authors' words, blatantly unfair to an individual.
span.quote: However, we demonstrate its inadequacy as a notion of fairness through several examples in which statistical parity is maintained, but from the point of view of an individual, the outcome is blatantly unfair

span.label: The metric the formal guarantee consumes is a social agreement that is expected to change.
span.quote: When ground truth is unavailable, the metric may reflect the “best” available approximation as agreed upon by society. Following established tradition [Raw01], the metric is assumed to be public and open to discussion and continual refinement

span.label: The bridge from individual fairness to group fairness holds only under a stated distance condition.
span.quote: we show that the Lipschitz condition implies statistical parity between two groups if and only if the Earthmover distance between the two groups is small

span.label: The population the metric is defined over is a modelling choice the authors flag.
span.quote: When dealing with the set V, we have assumed that V is the set of real individuals (rather than the potentially huge set of all possible encodings of individuals

span.label: differential-privacy tools and a Lipschitz metric formalism applied to define and enforce fairness in classification
span.quote: how tools developed in the context of differential privacy may be applied to fairness

span.label: statistical parity
span.quote: Statistical parity is the property that the demographics of those receiving positive (or negative) classifications are identical to the demographics of the population as a whole

span.label: group fairness
span.quote: Statistical parity speaks to group fairness rather than individual fairness

span.label: Lipschitz condition
span.quote: we show that the Lipschitz condition implies statistical parity between two groups if and only if the Earthmover distance between the two groups is small

span.label: Earthmover distance
span.quote: if and only if the Earthmover distance between the two groups is small

span.label: fairness through blindness
span.quote: fairness through blindness

span.label: fairness - INDIVIDUAL VERSUS GROUP, AND THE SECOND CAN HOLD WHILE THE FIRST FAILS: individual fairness is the principle that two people similar for a task be classified similarly, statistical parity is a property of demographics in aggregate, and the paper's examples keep the second while the first is blatantly violated
span.quote: Statistical parity speaks to group fairness rather than individual fairness, and appears desirable, as it equalizes outcomes across protected and non-protected groups

span.label: the similarity metric - AS SOCIETY'S CURRENT BEST APPROXIMATION: where no ground truth exists the metric stands in for one by agreement, is meant to be public and revisable, and is the input on which every formal result in the paper depends
span.quote: When ground truth is unavailable, the metric may reflect the “best” available approximation as agreed upon by society. Following established tradition [Raw01], the metric is assumed to be public and open to discussion and continual refinement

span.label: fairness as a principle - TREAT SIMILAR INDIVIDUALS SIMILARLY: the paper's whole notion is one sentence, and everything formal in it is machinery for making 'similar' precise, which is why the metric carries the weight rather than the definition
span.quote: We capture fairness by the principle that any two individuals who are similar with respect to a particular task should be classified similarly

span.label: contradicts → statistical parity as a notion of fairness
span.quote: statistical parity is maintained, but from the point of view of an individual, the outcome is blatantly unfair

span.label: builds-on → differential privacy (tools applied to fairness)
span.quote: tools developed in the context of differential privacy may be applied to fairness

span.label: extends → differential privacy [Dwo06, DMNS06]
span.quote: We observe that our definition of fairness is a generalization of the notion of differential privacy [Dwo06, DMNS06].

span.label: builds-on → the exponential mechanism [MT07]
span.quote: Our mechanism is based on the exponential mechanism [MT07], first considered in the context of differential privacy.

span.label: builds-on → the Earthmover relaxation for metric labeling and 0-extension [KT02, CKNZ04]
span.quote: The approach is inspired by the use of the Earthmover relaxation in the context of metric labeling and 0-extension [KT02, CKNZ04].

span.label: statistical parity —same-as→ group fairness
span.quote: Statistical parity speaks to group fairness rather than individual fairness, and appears desirable, as it equalizes outcomes across protected and non-protected groups

span.label: Lipschitz condition —causes→ statistical parity
span.note: holds when: only when the Earthmover distance between the two groups is small · strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: we show that the Lipschitz condition implies statistical parity between two groups if and only if the Earthmover distance between the two groups is small

span.label: Dwork et al. formalize INDIVIDUAL fairness as treat-similar-individuals-similarly via a task-specific similarity metric plus a Lipschitz condition on the randomized classifier, maximizing utility subject to that fairness constraint.
span.quote: an algorithm for maximizing utility subject to the fairness constraint, that similar individuals are treated similarly

span.label: An adaptation achieves fair affirmative action guaranteeing statistical parity (group demographics of any classification match the population), and the paper links fairness to differential privacy.
span.quote: which guarantees statistical parity (i.e., the demographics of the set of individuals receiving any classification are the same as the demographics of the underlying population)

span.quote: the fairness constraint, that similar individuals are treated similarly

span.quote: Clicking on such an ad may be strongly correlated with membership in S (even if exposure to the ad obeys statistical parity).

p.note: The full text of this article is not redistributable, so it is not included here. Every tag above carries the exact sentence it was made from, quoted under fair quotation. The article itself is at https://doi.org/10.1145/2090236.2090255.
